'''''Casuarina glauca''''', commonly known as '''swamp oak''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Karen |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=''Casuarina glauca'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Casuarina~glauca |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=1 May 2023}}</ref><ref name=ANBG>{{cite web |url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2005/casuarina-glauca.html |title=''Casuarina glauca'' prostrate forms |work=[[Australian National Botanic Gardens]]|publisher=Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=2023-09-12}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant that is [[endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is also known as '''swamp buloke''', '''swamp she-oak''', '''marsh sheoak''' or '''grey she-oak''',<ref name="foa">{{cite web |title=''Casuarina glauca'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Casuarina%20glauca |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=1 May 2023}}</ref> and is called '''guman''' by the [[Gadigal]] people in the [[Dharug language]].<ref name="RBGS" /> It is a [[Dioecy|dioecious]] tree that often forms [[Basal shoot|root suckers]] and has fissured and scaly bark, spreading or drooping branchlets, the leaves reduced to scales in [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] of 12 to 20, the fruit {{cvt|9–18|mm}} long containing winged seeds ([[Samara (fruit)|samara]]s) {{cvt|3.5–5.0|mm}} long.

==Description==
''Casuarina glauca'' is a dioecious tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|8–20|m}}, sometimes to {{cvt|35|m}}, rarely a shrub to about {{cvt|2|m}}, and that often forms root suckers. The bark is greyish brown, fissured and scaly. The branchlets are sometimes drooping, up to {{cvt|380|mm}} long, the leaves reduced to scale-like teeth about {{cvt|0.6–0.9|mm}} long, arranged in [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] of usually 12 to 17 around the branchlets, and long and curved back when young. The sections of branchlet between the leaf whorls (the "articles") are {{cvt|8–20|mm}} long and {{cvt|0.9–1.2|mm}} wide. 

Male flowers are arranged in spikes {{cvt|12–40|mm}} long in whorls of 7 to 10 per centimetre (per 0.4 inch) and the [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] about {{cvt|0.8|mm}} long. The female cones are on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|3–12|mm}} long and sparsely covered with soft, white to rust-coloured hairs when young. Mature cones are {{cvt|9–18|mm}} long and {{cvt|7–9|mm}} in diameter, the samaras {{cvt|3.5–5.0|mm}} long.<ref name="foa" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|page=84|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q2v3kb9tFsYC&pg=PA82}}</ref><ref name=Fairley>{{cite book |author1=Fairley, Alan |author2=Moore, Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |pages=64–65|location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Casuarina glauca'' was first formally described in 1826 by [[Kurt Polycarp Joachim Sprengel|Kurt Sprengel]] in ''[[Systema Vegetabilium]]'' from an unpublished description by [[Franz Sieber]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Casuarina glauca''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/458340|publisher=APNI|access-date=1 May 2023}}</ref><ref name="Spreng.">{{cite book |last1=Sprengel |first1=Kurt P.J. |title=Systema Vegetabilium|volume=3 |date=1826 |location=Göttingen |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15254#page/804/mode/1up |access-date=1 May 2023}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''glauca'') means '[[glaucous]]'.<ref name=enc>{{cite book |author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake, Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Vol. 2|year=1985|page=482|publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-143-5}}</ref>

The [[Gubbi Gubbi people|Kabi]] name for the plant, ''bilai'', was used for the town and locality of [[Bli Bli, Queensland]].<ref name=qpnt>{{cite QPN|3174|Bli Bli (town)|accessdate=25 June 2015}}</ref><ref name=qpnl>{{cite QPN|47165|Bli Bli (locality)|accessdate=25 June 2015}}</ref>

This species is closely related to ''C. cunninghamiana'',<ref name=2003Phylogenetics>{{Cite journal | last1=Steane | first1= Dorothy A. | last2= Wilson | first2= Karen L. | last3= Hill | first3= Robert S. | title= Using ''mat''K sequence data to unravel the phylogeny of Casuarinaceae | journal= Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution | volume= 28 | year= 2003 | issue= 1 | pages= 47–59 | url= http://eprints.utas.edu.au/3490/1/Acr664.pdf | doi= 10.1016/S1055-7903(03)00028-9 | pmid= 12801471 }}</ref> and hybrids with ''C. cunninghamiana'' subsp. ''cunninghamiana'' have been recorded where the two species co-occur, such as at [[Lower Portland, New South Wales|Lower Portland]] and [[Wisemans Ferry]].<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="benson">{{cite journal |last1=Benson |first1=Doug |last2=McDougall |first2=Lyn |title=Ecology of Sydney plant species Part3: Dicotyledon families Cabombaceae to Eupomat1aceae |journal=Cunninghamia |date=1995 |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=269–270 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/271021#page/131/mode/1up |access-date=1 May 2023}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Swamp she-oak is found along Australia's east coast from [[Yeppoon]] in central Queensland to [[Bermagui, New South Wales|Bermagui]] in southern New South Wales.<ref name="foa" /> Some stands within the Royal Botanic Gardens in Sydney predate European settlement.<ref name=benson/> Populations along the New South Wales coastline are at risk due to clearing of habitat for development.<ref name="RBGS"/> It has become highly invasive in Florida.<ref name=benson/>

''Casuarina glauca'' grows in or near brackish water along the banks of rivers and [[estuaries]]. Suckering from the roots, the swamp oak can form dense stands of trees.<ref name="foa" /> It grows on alluvial soils of sandstone or shale origin. The water table lies 30 cm or less under the surface. This tree then acts to turn shallows into land by preventing erosion and collecting material among its roots.<ref name=benson/> They are also a predominant species in the [[Coastal Swamp Oak Forest]]s in southeastern Australia.<ref>[http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/communities/pubs/141-conservation-advice.pdf Conservation advice (incorporating listing advice) for the Coastal Swamp Oak (''Casuarina glauca'') Forest of New South Wales and South East Queensland ecological community] ''[[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]]''. 20 March 2018. Retrieved 11 December 2023.</ref>

==Ecology==
''Casuarina glauca'' is an [[actinorhizal plant]] producing root nitrogen-fixing nodules infested by ''[[Frankia]]''. There is a regular pattern of cell layers containing [[flavan]]s.<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Laplaze | first1 = L. | last2 = Gherbi | first2 = H. | last3 = Frutz | first3 = T. | last4 = Pawlowski | first4 = K. | last5 = Franche | first5 = C. | last6 = Macheix | first6 = J. J. | last7 = Auguy | first7 = F. | last8 = Bogusz | first8 = D. | last9 = Duhoux | first9 = E. | chapter = Flavan-Containing Cells Delimit Frankia Infected Compartments in Casuarina glauca Nodules | doi = 10.1007/0-306-47615-0_254 | title = Nitrogen Fixation: From Molecules to Crop Productivity | series = Current Plant Science and Biotechnology in Agriculture | volume = 38 | pages = 455 | year = 2002 | isbn = 0-7923-6233-0 }}</ref> Although not a legume, ''C. glauca'', produces a [[hemoglobin]] (not a [[leghemoglobin]]) in its symbiotic root nodules.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Jacobsen-Lyon | first1 = K.| last2 = Jensen | first2 = E.O.| last3 = Jørgensen | first3 = J.E. | last4 = Marcker | first4 = K.A. | last5 = Peacock | first5 = W.J. | last6 = Dennis | first6 = E.S.| title = Symbiotic and nonsymbiotic hemoglobin genes of ''Casuarina glauca'' | journal = The Plant Cell | volume = 7 | issue = 2 | pages = 213–23 | year = 1995 | pmid = 7756831 | pmc = 160777 | doi=10.1105/tpc.7.2.213}}</ref>

The rat's tail orchid (''[[Dendrobium teretifolium]]'') grows on the swamp oak.<ref name=benson/>

It has become naturalised in the [[Everglades]] in Florida where it is considered a weed.<ref>{{cite web|title=Biological control of Australian native ''Casuarina'' species in the USA|url=http://www.csiro.au/science/ps334.html|work=Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation|access-date=16 September 2010|date=16 May 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605113952/http://www.csiro.au/science/ps334.html |archive-date=5 June 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

''C. glauca'' trees can live up to 200 years.<ref name=benson/>

Trees regenerate after fire by growing from the roots. Cut stumps sprout suckers vigorously, producing groves of new trees.<ref name=benson/> ''C. glauca'' trees drop large amounts of litter, mainly old cones and branchlets, which eventually rots down and enriches the soil unless removed by a flood event.<ref name=clark96/>

Understory plants recorded from swamp oak groves include ''[[Juncus kraussii]]'', ''[[Baumea juncea]]'' and ''[[Sporobolus virginicus]]'' on sandier soils and ''[[Apium prostratum]]'', ''[[Carex appressa]]'', ''[[Goodenia ovata]]'', ''Juncus kraussii'' and ''[[Phragmites australis]]'' and the vine ''[[Parsonsia straminea]]'' on clay soils.<ref name=clark96/>

[[Glossy black cockatoo]]s break the cones to eat the seeds, which mature in winter.<ref name=clark96>{{cite journal |url=http://www.une.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/35274/1996-clarke-allaway-aust-j-bot.pdf |author1=Clark, Peter J. |author2=Allaway, W.G. |year=1996 |journal=Australian Journal of Botany |title=Litterfall in ''Casuarina glauca'' Coastal Wetland Forests |volume=44 |issue=4 |pages=373–80 |doi=10.1071/bt9960373 |access-date=2016-05-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160820015056/http://www.une.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/35274/1996-clarke-allaway-aust-j-bot.pdf |archive-date=2016-08-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The seed is eaten by the [[red-browed finch]],<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.hornsby.nsw.gov.au/media/documents/environment-and-waste/bushland-and-biodiversity/native-tree-database-fact-sheets/Fact-sheet-Casuarina-glauca-Swamp-Oak.pdf | title=Casuarina glauca – Swamp Oak | author=Hornsby Shire Council | access-date=13 May 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160319104324/http://www.hornsby.nsw.gov.au/media/documents/environment-and-waste/bushland-and-biodiversity/native-tree-database-fact-sheets/Fact-sheet-Casuarina-glauca-Swamp-Oak.pdf | archive-date=19 March 2016 | url-status=dead }}</ref> and [[peaceful dove]] (''Geopelia placida'').<ref name="Barker 1984">{{cite book |author1=Barker, Robin Dale |author2=Vestjens, Wilhelmus Jacobus Maria | year = 1984 | title = The Food of Australian Birds: (I) Non-passerines | publisher = Melbourne University Press | isbn = 0-643-05007-8 | pages = 306|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Fh0RYPeTOz8C&pg=PA306}}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Casuarina glauca 'Cousin It'.jpg|thumb|'Cousin It' cultivar in [[Illawarra Grevillea Park]]]]
''Casuarina glauca'' has been planted widely as a street tree in Canberra.<ref name=bby>{{cite web|url=http://www.burkesbackyard.com.au/factsheets/Trees-and-Palms/Casuarinas/1338|title=Casuarinas | work=Burke's Backyard: Factsheets |author=Burke, Don |publisher=CTC Productions | access-date=11 May 2016}}</ref> It was introduced to Haiti to stabilise the soil and to be used as timber for poles, and to Florida where it was planted as an [[ornamental plant]] and windbreak.<ref name=benson/>

The bark has been used to plant orchids on.<ref name=enc/>

It tolerates waterlogged soils and even soils with some salinity. A significant inconvenience in urban settings is that its roots can invade underground water and sewer pipes if these are within 15 m (50 ft) of the tree.<ref name=bby/> It can also acidify acid sulphate soils as it lowers the water table.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/content/agriculture/resources/private-forestry/paddock-plants/Casuarina-glauca-Swamp-Sheoak.pdf | title=Swamp Oak or Swamp Sheoak | work=Paddock Plants Fact Sheets | date=1 November 2010 | access-date=13 May 2016 | author=Dept. Industry & Investment | publisher=New South Wales Government | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215002158/http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/content/agriculture/resources/private-forestry/paddock-plants/Casuarina-glauca-Swamp-Sheoak.pdf | archive-date=15 February 2017 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

Two prostrate forms are commercially available: ''Casuarina'' 'Cousin It' is a cultivar arising from material from [[Booderee National Park]] on the New South Wales south coast collected in 1989 and named for its resemblance to [[Cousin Itt]],<ref name=Growing-Native-Plants>{{Cite web |author=Hitchcock, Bobbie | orig-year= 2005 | title=''Casuarina glauca'' prostrate forms| url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2005/casuarina-glauca.html | work= Growing Native Plants | version= (online version at www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/) | publisher= Australian National Botanic Gardens, Australian Government | date=24 December 2015 | location= Canberra, Australian Capital Territory | access-date= 11 May 2016}}</ref> and ''C.'' ‘Kattang Karpet’ is propagated by the Australian Botanic Garden from material collected at [[Kattang Nature Reserve]] on the New South Wales mid-north coast in 1998.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/Plants/Gardening/Growing-Prostrate-Casurina-Glauca-Forms | title=Growing Prostrate Casuarina Glauca Forms | work=Gardening | author=Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney | publisher=State of New South Wales and Office of Environment and Heritage |access-date=11 May 2016}}</ref>
